title: Lot sizes

inOneLine.simple: A lot is the unit for trade size. Bigger lots mean each pip is worth more money.
inOneLine.balanced: By common convention 1.00 [[lot]] is 100,000 units of the [[base-currency]], 0.10 is 10,000 and 0.01 is 1,000, but your broker's [[contract-size]] decides the real number.

explain.simple: You choose your trade size in lots. Usually a standard lot is 100,000 units of the first currency in the pair. A mini lot (0.10) is 10,000 units. A micro lot (0.01) is 1,000 units. MetaTrader calls the size 'volume' and shows it in lots. Brokers can use a different contract size, so check it for each symbol before you trade.
explain.balanced: Size in units = lots × [[contract-size]]. With the common 100,000-unit contract, 0.25 lots is 25,000 units of the base currency. The size you pick sets how much each [[pip]] is worth and how much [[margin]] the trade needs. The smallest size and the size steps allowed also depend on the broker.

assumptions: Contract size 100,000 units per lot (check your broker)
Trade on EUR/USD, so the units are euros
A made-up broker symbol whose contract specification says 10,000 units per lot
This is only to show why checking matters; it is not any real broker's setting
steps: The same 'lot' number gives a size ten times smaller than with a 100,000-unit contract, so pip value and margin are ten times smaller too.

explainSimpler: Lots are like box sizes. A standard box holds 100,000, a mini box 10,000, and a micro box 1,000. Check the label on your broker's boxes.
commonMistake: Thinking 1.00 lot is a small trade because the number looks small. With a 100,000-unit contract, 1.00 lot on EUR/USD moves about 10 USD per pip. Start practice with 0.01 lots and always check the contract size.

quickCheck.prompt: With a 100,000-unit contract, how many units is 0.05 lots?
Where should you check how many units one lot is for a symbol?

options.text: Your broker's contract specification for that symbol
options.explanation: Right: the broker sets the contract size, and it can differ between symbols.

options.text: Nowhere: one lot is always 100,000 units everywhere
options.explanation: No: 100,000 is a common convention, not a rule every broker follows.

doItNow.instructions: Open the pip value calculator. Enter EUR/USD with 0.01, 0.10 and 1.00 lots and a 100,000-unit contract. Write down the pip value for each and notice how it grows with size.

homework: Find your demo broker's contract specification for EUR/USD (often on its website) and write down the contract size and the smallest volume allowed.
